# Testing: Unit, Integration, and Systests {#sec-testing}

::: {.callout-note title="Status: complete first draft"}
:::

A streaming engine has more interesting failure modes than most
software. Watermarks can be off-by-one. Window state can leak.
Joins can produce duplicates. JIT-compiled code can produce wrong
answers that depend on the input distribution. Without good tests,
none of this is caught before users see wrong results.

NebulaStream's test infrastructure is in three layers:

- **Unit tests** — Google Test on individual classes, in
  per-module `tests/` directories.
- **Integration tests** — multi-component tests using the
  `nes-coordinator-test-util` helpers.
- **System tests (systests)** — declarative `.test` files that
  describe a query plus expected output, run end-to-end against
  the worker.

The systests are the most distinctive piece. This chapter walks
through each layer with the most attention on systests.

---

## 20.1 The unit-test setup {#sec-unit-tests}

Each `nes-*` module that has tests has them in a `tests/`
subdirectory. The CMake helpers in
`/Users/zeuchste/git/nebulastream/cmake/NebulaStreamTest.cmake`
make registration trivial:

```cmake
# cmake/NebulaStreamTest.cmake
function(add_nes_integration_test)
    add_executable(${ARGN})
    set(TARGET_NAME ${ARGV0})
    add_dependencies(integration_tests ${TARGET_NAME})
    target_precompile_headers(${TARGET_NAME} REUSE_FROM nes-common)
    target_link_libraries(${TARGET_NAME} nes-coordinator-test-util)
    gtest_discover_tests(${TARGET_NAME} WORKING_DIRECTORY ${CMAKE_CURRENT_BINARY_DIR})
endfunction()
```

There are three test helpers, distinguished by what they link
against:

- `add_nes_unit_test` — links `nes-data-types`. The smallest
  surface; for tests of pure-function utilities like type
  inference or schema manipulation.
- `add_nes_common_test` — links `nes-common`. For tests that
  need logging, identifiers, exceptions.
- `add_nes_integration_test` — links `nes-coordinator-test-util`.
  For tests that need the full engine, with fake sources and
  sinks.

Tests run through CTest:

```shell
ctest --test-dir cmake-build-debug -j --output-on-failure
ctest --test-dir cmake-build-debug -R "DecideJoinTypesTest" --output-on-failure
```

The discovery is automatic — `gtest_discover_tests` finds all the
`TEST` and `TEST_F` macros in the binary and registers them with
CTest at build time.

Most operator-internal logic is unit-tested. The pace of unit
tests is high; you can run all of them in under a minute.

---

## 20.2 The systest framework {#sec-systests}

The interesting layer is the systest framework. Systests are
declarative `.test` files that describe a complete query — schema,
data, query, expected output — in a single readable document. The
worker runs the query against a fake source carrying the inline
data and the test framework checks the actual output against the
expected.

A small example:

```sql
# nes-systests/tuples/FiveTuples.test
# name: sources/FiveTuples.test
# description: Simple source/buffer tests
# groups: [Tuples]

CREATE LOGICAL SOURCE fiveTuples(field_1 UINT64 NOT NULL);
CREATE PHYSICAL SOURCE FOR fiveTuples TYPE File;
ATTACH INLINE
1
2
3
4
5

CREATE SINK sinkFiveTuples(...)  TYPE File;
SELECT field_1 FROM fiveTuples INTO sinkFiveTuples;
----
1
2
3
4
5
```

Three sections separated by `----`:

1. **Metadata** (`# name:`, `# description:`, `# groups:`).
2. **Setup + query** (the SQL, with `ATTACH INLINE` to embed input
   data directly in the file).
3. **Expected output** (after `----`).

The framework runs the query and asserts the actual output
matches the expected, ignoring trailing whitespace.

This format is brilliant for streaming engines. Streaming queries
have multiple inputs, time-dependent behaviour, and complex
expected outputs that are tedious to express in unit tests.
Putting everything in one file — schema, input, query, expected
— makes the test self-documenting.

---

## 20.3 The systest CLI {#sec-systest-cli}

Systests run through a dedicated `systest` executable. From
CLAUDE.md:

```shell
# Build the systest binary
cmake --build cmake-build-debug --target systest

# Run a single systest file
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest -t nes-systests/operator/join/HashJoin.test

# Run a specific case within a file
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest \
    -t nes-systests/function/arithmetical/FunctionAdd.test:1
```

The `:N` suffix runs only the Nth query in the file. Files with
multiple queries are common — a single `.test` file might contain
five variations on a theme, each numbered.

The systest binary builds the engine in-process and runs each
query against the test's input. Setup and teardown are
test-local; failures are reported per-query with a diff against
the expected output.

You can pass worker configuration overrides after `--`:

```shell
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest \
    -t nes-systests/operator/join/JoinMultipleStreams.test:1 \
    -- --worker.default_query_execution.execution_mode=INTERPRETER
```

This is what most of this book's reading exercises do. Switching
between COMPILER and INTERPRETER mode is the primary tool for
isolating JIT bugs from operator-logic bugs.

---

## 20.4 Multi-worker testing {#sec-multi-worker-testing}

The systest harness supports running queries against multiple
worker processes simultaneously. The CI configuration starts
parallel workers in Docker containers — vanilla, profiler-
instrumented, coverage-instrumented, sanitizer-equipped — on
ports 8080, 8081, 8082, 8083. A single `.test` file's queries
are dispatched across them; the same query runs in each worker
and the framework asserts that all workers produce the same
expected output.

This is *not yet* the same thing as a true distributed-systest
suite. It is parallel execution of single-node queries against
identical-but-instrumented workers, primarily to catch
sanitizer-only bugs. Genuine multi-worker scenarios — where
operators of one query are placed across multiple workers
(Chapter 19) — are exercised through dedicated coordinator
integration tests that live outside `nes-systests/`.

The closest thing to a distributed scenario in the systest
suite as of `origin/main` is
`nes-systests/benchmark/ClusterMonitoring.test`, a multi-stream
monitoring workload modelled on the Google cluster-trace
dataset. Even this runs single-node by default; the cluster
shape comes from the input data, not from running across
workers.

Filling the distributed-systest gap is on the engine's
near-term roadmap (Chapter 22 mentions it as one of the items
the QueryManager work blocks).

## 20.5 Group tags and CI integration {#sec-systest-groups}

The metadata header allows tests to belong to *groups*. The
group tag `[fast]` means the test runs in the fast lane of CI,
which executes on every PR. `[nightly]` (or `.test_nightly`
suffix) means the test runs only on nightly builds. Other tags
(e.g., `[legacy]`, `[join]`) help filter test runs:

```shell
# Run all tests in the join group
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest --groups=join
```

The CI matrix from CLAUDE.md is detailed: every PR triggers
format check → smoke tests → full matrix (x86_64/arm64 ×
libcxx/libstdcxx × Debug/RelWithDebInfo/Release × address/
undefined/thread/none sanitizers) plus clang-tidy diff plus code
coverage. The systests run within this matrix; sanitizer-equipped
runs catch a lot of bugs that pure unit tests miss.

---

## 20.5 Why systests are documentation {#sec-systests-as-docs}

The systests double as living documentation of the engine's
behaviour. A new contributor wanting to know "what is the exact
syntax for a windowed aggregation" can grep the systests and find
a working example. We have, throughout this book, used systest
file paths as the targets of "Reading Exercise" sidebars,
because:

- Every systest file is self-contained.
- Every systest file is tested in CI; it cannot be wrong without
  CI noticing.
- Every systest file is a real example of a real query that the
  engine actually runs.

For an instructor using this book as a course text, the systests
are an inexhaustible source of homework: every test file is a
small puzzle the student can run, modify, and predict the output
for.

---

## 20.6 What is hard to test {#sec-hard-to-test}

A few testing problems have no clean solution today:

- **Timing-dependent behaviour.** A windowed aggregation's exact
  firing time depends on real-time progress; deterministic tests
  use synthetic timestamps embedded in the input, but
  edge-case timing bugs can still escape.
- **Long-running workloads.** Memory leaks that show up only after
  hours of continuous operation are not caught by tests that run
  for seconds.
- **Concurrency bugs in the JIT.** Race conditions in JIT-compiled
  code may not reproduce reliably; ThreadSanitizer helps but is
  not a silver bullet.
- **Numerical edge cases in user-defined functions.** A UDF that
  divides by a value that happens to be zero only on one machine's
  data is hard to test without running on that data.

The engine compensates with the sanitizer matrix and a
substantial nightly test budget, but the testing-frontier
problems are real.

---

## Summary {#sec-ch20-summary}

NebulaStream's testing has three layers: unit tests via Google
Test in per-module `tests/` directories; integration tests via
`nes-coordinator-test-util`; and system tests via the declarative
`.test` file format that describes schema, input data, query, and
expected output in a single document. Systests double as
self-documenting examples and are the primary target of this
book's reading exercises. The CI matrix runs the full test suite
across architectures, libcxx flavours, build types, and
sanitizers, providing strong coverage even of timing-sensitive
bugs that pure unit tests would miss.

---

## Reading exercises {#sec-ch20-exercises}

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 20.1: read three systests"}
Open three systests in `nes-systests/`:

- `nes-systests/tuples/FiveTuples.test` (a trivial source-to-sink
  test).
- `nes-systests/operator/join/JoinMultipleStreams.test` (a
  multi-stream join).
- A windowed-aggregation test of your choice from
  `nes-systests/windows/`.

For each, identify the schema, the input, the query, and the
expected output. Trace through what the engine does to produce
the expected output.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 20.2: write your own"}
Construct a `.test` file for a query of your own design. Stay
small: 5 input rows, one filter, one projection. Run it:

```shell
cmake-build-debug/systest/systest -t /path/to/my-test.test
```

Iterate until it passes. Then add a deliberate bug — predict an
output that is wrong by one row — and run again. The diff in
the failure message is exactly what you would see on a real CI
failure.
:::

::: {.callout-important title="Reading exercise 20.3: systests across modes"}
Pick any operator systest. Run it three times: COMPILER mode,
INTERPRETER mode, and with one of the sanitizers enabled. Are
the answers the same? They should be. If they are not, you have
found a real bug.
:::
